headline: Where does your system actually need to be?
blurb: Most stats feel wrong because they're built one tier too low — or one tier too high. Answer a few questions, find your rung on the ladder, then see what it costs, why it works, the pain that tells you to climb, and how to build it.

questions.text: What is the most advanced question you need to answer about this number?

options.label: Just its value right now
options.hint: how many contacts / open jobs / current pipeline

options.label: How it has changed over time
options.hint: trends, vs last month, charts over months

options.label: Rates, conversion, flow — or attribution that survives edits
options.hint: close rate, time-to-close, profit by source

options.label: What any record looked like at an arbitrary past moment
options.hint: full audit, replay, "what did we believe at time T"

questions.text: How heavily is this number read versus how often the data changes?

options.label: Read occasionally — fine to compute live
Read constantly / on hot pages / under load
options.hint: it shows up in latency or DB load

questions.text: If a single underlying event were silently lost, what is the impact?

options.label: Negligible — it is directional
options.hint: a glance, a trend, a vanity funnel

options.label: It would throw off money, commissions, or a real decision

questions.text: Where do the events come from / who needs them?

options.label: Other services need to consume them

warnings.insight_pairing: Insight-grade — you can keep collection light and fast; approximate is fine here.
warnings.money_pairing: Money-grade on a durable level — your numbers will be exact and recoverable. Good pairing.
warnings.sourcing_floor: Event sourcing needs a durable floor — Level 3 minimum. Lossy collection can't be the source of truth.
warnings.money_vs_lossy: Money-grade events can't live on the lossy telemetry sink — it silently drops data you'd need to reconcile. Route them through the durable outbox (Level 3), and keep anonymous telemetry as a separate sink that stitches to your business events at conversion.

1.name: Live query on current state
1.tagline: Compute it on demand from rows as they exist now.
1.captures: The current value, exact to the second. "How many contacts," "open jobs," "current pipeline."
1.why: Always correct, zero infrastructure, nothing to invalidate. The right answer far more often than people think.
1.pains: No history — the table only knows now. Deletes and edits erase the past. Cannot answer "how many last March."
1.avoid: Raise timeouts, throw hardware at the DB, sprinkle ad-hoc view caching.
1.avoid_pain: Mystery slow pages and a count query that quietly becomes the app bottleneck.

build_steps.title: That is the whole tier
build_steps.code: # no job, no table, no cache. climb only when a trigger below fires.

2.name: Cached current state
2.tagline: The same value, memoized so the read is cheap.
2.captures: Same questions as Tier 1, at scale or on hot paths.
2.why: Fast reads. counter_cache is the clean form — the framework keeps the number current as rows come and go, so reads are free.
2.pains: Still no history. New risk: a cache that drifts if invalidation is wrong. Freshness becomes a choice, not a guarantee.
2.avoid: Cache it manually in fifty places with no single invalidation path.
2.avoid_pain: Stale numbers nobody trusts and bugs you can never reproduce.

build_steps.title: counter_cache — the clean version
build_steps.code:
class Job < ApplicationRecord
  belongs_to :contact, counter_cache: true
end
# migration: add_column :contacts, :jobs_count, :integer, default: 0
# backfill: Contact.find_each { |c| Contact.reset_counters(c.id, :jobs) }

build_steps.title: Or a Redis counter for cross-cutting totals
build_steps.code:
# on write
$redis.incr("open_jobs")   # decr on close
# on read
$redis.get("open_jobs").to_i

build_steps.title: Or a materialized view on a refresh schedule

3.name: Periodic snapshot
3.tagline: A scheduled job writes the current value to a history table.
3.setup: a scheduled job + a metrics table
3.maintenance: the cron job; backfilling gaps when a run fails
3.captures: Trends of a level over time: "contacts at each month-end," "pipeline over the year."
3.why: First tier that creates history the current-state tables can't reconstruct. Deleting a contact never touches yesterday's snapshot.
3.pains: Granularity is fixed by cadence — daily means no hourly, ever. Captures levels, lies about flow: 3 created + 2 deleted shows as +1, and the 3 and 2 are gone.
3.avoid: Keep soft-deleted rows forever to reconstruct history; track numbers by hand in a spreadsheet.
3.avoid_pain: Bloated tables, "deleted" data leaking into live queries, and a spreadsheet that becomes the real (always-stale) source of truth.

build_steps.title: A history table keyed by date
build_steps.code:
create_table :daily_metrics do |t|
  t.date :as_of, null: false
  t.integer :contacts, :open_jobs
  t.bigint :pipeline_cents
end
add_index :daily_metrics, :as_of, unique: true

build_steps.title: A nightly job that samples current state
build_steps.code:
class SnapshotJob
  def perform
    DailyMetric.upsert({
      as_of: Date.today,
      contacts: Contact.count,
      open_jobs: Job.open.count,
      pipeline_cents: Job.open.sum(:value_cents)
    }, unique_by: :as_of)
  end
end

4.name: Event log + rollups
4.tagline: Record every occurrence as an immutable event; aggregate from it.
4.setup: event defs · emission at each change · events table · rollups · registry
4.captures: Flow and causality exactly — every thing that happened, in order, with its values frozen. Rates, conversion, time-between-states, drift-proof attribution.
4.why: The churn problem disappears (you see the 3 and the 2). Attribution survives later edits because the value was copied into the event, not pointed at. Any new breakdown is just a re-aggregation.
4.pains: You only get the dimensions you snapshotted into the payload. Records what happened; does not rebuild an entity's arbitrary past state. Most moving parts so far.
4.avoid: Compute rates from same-period snapshots (this-month closes ÷ this-month leads); store the daily ratio instead of its two counts; derive "events" by diffing state at end of day.
4.avoid_pain: Metrics that invert under volume, average-of-averages errors, and a corrupt event log with fabricated timestamps — the "feels wrong because it IS wrong" problem.

build_steps.title: Define the event (schema-first)
build_steps.code:
class DealClosed < EventDefinition
  required_payload :lead_id, :salesperson_id, :source_id
  required_payload :amount_cents
  # occurred_at (spine) = when it happened
end

build_steps.title: Emit at the moment of the change — freeze the values
build_steps.code:
def close_deal!(deal)
  deal.update!(state: :won)
  emit :deal_closed,
    lead_id: deal.lead_id, salesperson_id: deal.rep_id,
    source_id: deal.lead.source_id,   # frozen NOW, survives later edits
    amount_cents: deal.total_cents
end

build_steps.title: Project into a permanent, queryable events table
build_steps.code:
create_table :events do |t|
  t.uuid :event_id; t.string :name
  t.datetime :occurred_at
  t.bigint :source_id, :salesperson_id  # promoted = filterable
  t.bigint :amount_cents
  t.jsonb :payload
end
add_index :events, :event_id, unique: true
add_index :events, [:name, :occurred_at]

build_steps.title: Roll up by recomputation (idempotent, auditable)
build_steps.code:
INSERT INTO sales_rollups (period, source_id, deals, revenue_cents)
SELECT date_trunc('month', occurred_at), source_id,
  count(*), sum(amount_cents)
FROM events WHERE name = 'deal_closed'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ON CONFLICT (period, source_id) DO UPDATE SET ...;

build_steps.title: Reconcile — the recompute is the auditor
build_steps.code:
# nightly: rebuild from events, diff vs incremental rollup.
# any mismatch = a caught bug. unique event_id stops double-counting.

5.name: Event sourcing
5.tagline: Events ARE the record; state is a projection you replay.
5.captures: Everything Tier 4 does, plus arbitrary past state and full audit replay — questions you never anticipated.
5.why: One source of truth. Reconstruct any moment. Fix a projection and re-derive it cleanly. Strongest possible audit position.
5.pains: Heaviest to build and reason about. Overkill for most data. Replay and old-event versioning become permanent concerns. Resist it unless you truly need reconstruction or regulatory replay.
5.avoid: Bolt on an audit_log; add history columns ad hoc; keep a changes table.
5.avoid_pain: Partial history covering only what you anticipated, audit gaps exactly where you didn't log, two sources of truth that disagree.

build_steps.title: Events are the only writes
build_steps.code:
# never UPDATE state. append facts.
store.append(deal_id, :deal_closed, amount_cents: 1_850_000)

build_steps.title: State is folded from the stream
build_steps.code:
def rebuild(deal_id)
  store.events_for(deal_id).reduce(Deal.new) do |deal, event|
    deal.apply(event)   # pure function: (state, event) -> state
  end
end

build_steps.title: Snapshot for replay speed; query as-of any date
build_steps.code:
# "what did this look like on 2026-03-31?"
store.events_for(deal_id, before: Date.new(2026, 3, 31)).reduce(...)
